elements.element: Customer may terminate the Agreement or an Order Form for convenience.
elements.evidence: Revised 14.2.2 reads "PB may terminate this Agreement for convenience, without cause, at any time..." The prior gating conditions (only after SFJ paid/incurred $60 million of Development Costs and only prior to first Regulatory Approval) are deleted, so the election is unconditional. There are no Order Forms in this Co-Development Agreement, so agreement-level termination is the full scope of the element. The deterministic check "Customer convenience termination present = false" is a lexical artefact (the customer is aliased "PB", not "Customer"); on substance the grant is present.

elements.element: Customer's convenience termination requires no more than 30 days' written notice.
elements.evidence: "upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice to SFJ" replaces the redacted blank "[***] prior written notice", fixing the undefined trigger and setting notice at exactly 30 days.

elements.element: Vendor refunds prepaid fees pro rata after Customer's convenience termination.
elements.evidence: "SFJ will refund pro rata any fees or other amounts prepaid by PB for the period after the effective date of termination." The refund is expressly pro rata (not merely post-termination-period), runs from Vendor to Customer, and is tied to the convenience termination in the same sentence.

elements.element: Vendor has no right to terminate for convenience during a committed term.
elements.evidence: New sentence: "SFJ has no right to terminate this Agreement for convenience during the Term." "Term" is a defined concept (1.1.185 / Section 14.1), so the temporal anchor is not undefined. Retained SFJ exits are trigger-conditioned rather than at will (14.2.6 requires a Change of Control; 14.2.10 requires PB's exercise of Section 5.2.4 decision-making plus failed Executive Officer escalation; MAE, bankruptcy, safety, compliance-breach and Adverse Patent Impact rights are all event-based), so no retained sentence contradicts the new prohibition.

elements.element: Customer may terminate for convenience on 60 to 90 days' notice.
elements.evidence: Notice is set at thirty (30) days, below the 60-90 day fallback band. This is a deliberate (and customer-favourable) choice at the preferred level, not a fallback defect, but the fallback element as written is not satisfied.

elements.element: Any early-termination fee is capped at three months of fees.
elements.evidence: The retained third sentence keeps "an amount equal to three hundred percent (300%) of Development Costs paid or incurred by SFJ prior to such termination", plus continuing Approval Payments under ARTICLE 6. No three-months-of-fees cap exists and the Agreement has no fee-period concept to measure one against.

elements.element: Vendor may terminate for convenience only at the end of a term.
elements.evidence: Satisfied a fortiori: "SFJ has no right to terminate this Agreement for convenience during the Term" removes any mid-term Vendor convenience exit, which is at least as restrictive as an end-of-term-only right.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 90 days' notice of convenience termination.
elements.evidence: Conditional element whose condition does not apply: SFJ holds no convenience termination right at all under the revised 14.2.2, so no Vendor convenience notice period is required. All retained SFJ exits are cause/event-triggered and fall outside T4C.

reasons: Position-complete at the preferred level: all four preferred elements are met in operative language (express unconditional PB convenience right, 30 days' written notice, pro rata refund of prepayments, express bar on SFJ convenience termination during the Term). The fallback is incomplete (30 days is outside the 60-90 band; no three-months-of-fees cap against the retained 300% Development Cost payment), but completeness at either level suffices.

The single deterministic failure ("Customer convenience termination present") is a naming artefact: the checker looks for "Customer" while this Agreement aliases the customer as "PB". Substantively the grant, notice period and refund all appear in the rendered clause, so the failure should not be read as a coverage gap.

Minimality holds. The deletions ($60 million Development Cost gate, the pre-first-Regulatory-Approval cut-off, the blank [***] notice figure) are exactly the terms that defeated elements 1 and 2; nothing outside the checklist was cut. The 300% Trial Data Package payment, the ARTICLE 6 Approval Payment carry-over, the Section 6.2/6.7 adjustments and the clause heading are all retained verbatim. No survival tail, expense allocation, procedure or extra damages category was added.

The words "or other amounts" in the refund limb are a modest broadening beyond "prepaid fees", but they are functionally necessary rather than an extra: this Agreement defines no "fees", operating instead on Development Costs, Approval Payments and the Buy-Out Payment, so a fees-only refund would be a nullity. "without cause" alongside "for convenience" is redundant phrasing but is not a substantive addition.

Intent is preserved. The consideration architecture is untouched: PB still purchases the Trial Data Package under Section 11.1.1.4 for 300% of Development Costs, still owes Approval Payments if it continues development and obtains approval, and the Section 6.2 adjustment and set-off for amounts previously paid under 14.2.2 survive. No cross-reference is left dangling and no defined term is orphaned.

Watch-item for the drafter (not a defect at the preferred level): because the pre-approval window is deleted, PB can now invoke 14.2.2 after Regulatory Approval, in which case the retained sentence "if PB elects to continue development of the Product and obtains Regulatory Approval following such termination" is merely inapposite rather than contradictory. If SFJ pushes back, confirm expressly that the 300% payment and Approval Payment carry-over apply on any 14.2.2 exercise regardless of approval timing.

Commercial flag consistent with the margin comment: the exit is now unconditional but not free (300% of Development Costs plus continuing Approval Payments). The preferred checklist contains no fee-cap element, so this is correctly raised in the rationale rather than redlined here; if the team wants price relief it should be negotiated as a separate ask, not folded into this operation.
